central_question: Could the body’s most inconvenient dashboard light be a reason to check cardiovascular risk?
thesis: Erections partly depend on blood flow, so persistent erectile changes can be a useful prompt to review blood pressure and cardiometabolic health—not merely shop for a performance fix.
hook: “Your body has a dashboard. Apparently, it installed one warning light in a very inconvenient place.” Open on a flawless luxury-car interior: one tiny warning beacon flashes while Satoshi calmly pretends it is decorative.
audience_objection: “Isn’t that wildly alarmist? ED can come from stress, anxiety, medication, diabetes, or plenty of other things.” Answer it fast: exactly—this is not a diagnosis, which is why the sensible move is a real check rather than self-diagnosis or panic-buying.

escalation.visual: Satoshi covers the dashboard beacon with tape; smash cut to a shopping basket overflowing with powders, pills, gummies, and confidence-branded moon dust.
escalation.turn: The first instinct is to buy a solution for the symptom before asking why the light came on.

escalation.visual: Dive through an abstract, stylized blood vessel where traffic begins to bunch up.
escalation.turn: Erectile function involves blood flow; persistent ED is associated with higher cardiovascular and atherosclerotic risk.

escalation.visual: The vessel traffic freezes; a clean split-screen shows a calm checklist replacing the shopping basket.
escalation.turn: The awkward symptom is not necessarily the problem to hide—it may be the clue that gets the wider system checked.

escalation.visual: Checklist: blood pressure, blood sugar/metabolic risk, cholesterol, medications, stress. Return to the small dashboard light.
escalation.turn: The payoff is boringly powerful: do maintenance, not magical thinking.

key_receipt: Primary prospective evidence from MESA found self-reported ED associated with later cardiovascular events after adjustment (Uddin et al., Circulation, 2018); a meta-analysis of 12 prospective cohorts found similar associations (Dong et al., JACC, 2011). NHLBI identifies ED as a possible early warning sign of elevated atherosclerosis risk, while NIDDK documents its many vascular and nonvascular causes.
payoff: “A dashboard light is not a diagnosis. But if it keeps coming on, maybe don’t buy another air freshener for the car. Check the engine.” End on the beacon blinking—not ominously, just too important to tape over.
mens_health_bridge: This reframes men’s health from performance anxiety and product-chasing to systems maintenance: sexual function, blood pressure, metabolic health, medication effects, and stress belong in the same grown-up conversation.
tone: Dryly funny, composed, visually luxurious, non-shaming; the joke targets denial and wellness marketing, never the person experiencing ED.

cuts.visual: Luxury dashboard; tiny warning beacon flashes.
Satoshi tries tape over the light; deadpan pause.
Absurd wellness-product basket fills the frame.
Rapid, clean labels: stress, anxiety, medicines, diabetes, vascular issues.
cuts.purpose: Defuse diagnostic certainty without slowing the story.

cuts.visual: The basket disappears; calm clinician-style checklist appears.
cuts.purpose: Offer the useful alternative: blood pressure and cardiometabolic review.

cuts.visual: Return to dashboard; the light remains visible as the car drives smoothly into daylight. End card carries NHLBI, NIDDK, MESA, and Princeton IV citations.
cuts.purpose: Land the callback: not catastrophe, maintenance.

one_boundary_sentence: Persistent ED can have many causes and does not diagnose heart disease, but it can be a reason to review cardiovascular risk.
